abstract: |
  **Objectives:** This study examines the consequences of the New York City Police Department’s late-2022 operational shift that sharply expanded vehicle pursuits without a formal policy change. We evaluate whether the surge in pursuits affected motor vehicle collisions, robberies, and shootings, and whether any crime-prevention benefits offset the associated collision costs.
  **Methods:** For collision outcomes, interrupted time series (ITS) segmented regression provides direct causal estimates. For crime outcomes, where within-city trends may reflect national forces, we triangulate across a city-level ITS, a generalized synthetic control comparing New York with large U.S. cities, a test of whether crime rose after the February 2025 re-restriction, and descriptive borough- and precinct-level comparisons of where any decline was concentrated. A cost-benefit analysis estimates the threshold of prevented shootings needed for pursuit escalation to break even.
  **Results:** Monthly pursuits rose from roughly eight to a peak above 200. Pursuit-related collisions increased proportionally with pursuit volume across all four policy regimes and declined sharply following the February 2025 policy re-restriction. The collision result is the paper's one causally identified estimate. Crime outcomes provide no evidence of deterrence. The generalized synthetic control finds NYC's post-2022 shooting trajectory statistically indistinguishable from the national counterfactual, and robbery, if anything, rose relative to comparable cities. The February 2025 reduction in pursuits was not followed by any increase in crime. Descriptive within-city comparisons align: the shooting DiD rests on non-parallel pre-trends, and the robbery DiD runs opposite to deterrence.
  **Conclusions:** Pursuit escalation produced clear and attributable collision harms while providing no credible evidence of crime reduction. Cost-benefit estimates suggest the threshold of prevented shootings required to offset these harms was not achieved. Agencies should require affirmative evidence of crime-prevention benefits before expanding pursuit authority.

# Introduction

Vehicle pursuits are among the most dangerous activities in American policing. From 2009 to 2023, pursuit-related crashes in the United States killed an average of 423 people per year, and roughly one-third of those killed were bystanders with no involvement in the chase [@Hendrix2026; @rivara2004motor]. Adjusting for population and overall crash volume, pursuit fatality risk rose approximately 2% annually over that period, and deaths cluster in identifiable settings — urban areas, nighttime hours, and non-interstate roads [@Hendrix2026; see also @alpert1986most; @hill2002high]. Police departments have been writing and rewriting pursuit policies for decades, under substantial public pressure and with remarkably little empirical guidance [@alpert1997pucker; @hicks2003police].

Despite the stakes, empirical evidence on the effects of pursuit policy changes remains thin. Case studies show that pursuit frequency responds sharply to policy, but none has rigorously estimated the resulting effects on crime, collisions, and public safety using modern causal methods. The question that @rivara2004motor posed two decades ago — whether "the trade-off of fewer pursuit-related crashes and deaths [is] offset by a higher number of fatal crimes" — remains unanswered.

The New York City Police Department's experience beginning in late 2022 offers a rare opportunity to address this question. Under Mayor Eric Adams's quality-of-life enforcement mandate and new Chief of Patrol John Chell, the NYPD dramatically escalated its use of vehicle pursuits without any formal revision to the department's written Patrol Guide procedure on pursuits. Monthly pursuits rose from an average of eight before the escalation to more than 200 at their peak, a 25-fold increase. Two further policy changes followed. In August 2023, Chief of Department Jeffrey Maddrey issued a compliance memo, and in February 2025, Commissioner Jessica Tisch formally revised the policy to permit pursuits only for felonies and violent misdemeanors. The result is a multi-phase natural experiment in which pursuit intensity varied dramatically across distinct policy regimes within a single jurisdiction.

We exploit this variation to estimate the effects of pursuit escalation on motor vehicle collisions, robberies, and gun violence. For collision outcomes, the causal pathway is direct and theoretically unambiguous: more pursuits create more collision risk. An interrupted time-series (ITS) model provides well-identified causal estimates. The collision finding is the paper's primary causal contribution.

Crime outcomes pose a harder identification problem because within-city trends may reflect secular forces unrelated to pursuit policy. We therefore triangulate across city- and borough-level time-series analyses, a precinct-level heterogeneity design, and a national comparison. We also examine whether crime increased after the February 2025 restriction sharply reduced pursuits, providing an internal test of the deterrence mechanism.

# Background

## Vehicle Pursuit Policy in American Policing

Police vehicle pursuits have been a subject of scholarly and legal scrutiny since the mid-1980s, when @alpert1986most described the police vehicle as "the most deadly force" in an officer's arsenal. Despite the risks, pursuit policy remained largely unregulated through the early 1980s, with most departments permitting officers broad discretion to initiate and continue pursuits [@kennedy1992comparative]. The first wave of reform resulted from mounting civil liability under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which exposed departments to lawsuits when pursuits resulted in injuries to bystanders or suspects [@alpert1997constitutional; @oconnor2005police].

By the late 1990s, pursuit policies had coalesced around three general types [@alpert1997pucker; @kenney1997national]. *Judgmental* policies grant officers wide discretion to engage in pursuits based on their assessment of the situation. *Restrictive* policies limit pursuits to specific offense categories (typically violent felonies) and impose conditions related to speed, traffic density, and weather. *Discouragement* policies formally permit pursuits but establish a strong institutional presumption against them, coupled with mandatory supervisory review and potential discipline. A 1997 national survey of 436 agencies found that 48% had revised pursuit policies within the preceding two years (87% toward greater restrictions), yet variation persisted. Some agencies reported zero annual pursuits, others over 800 [@kenney1997national].

The literature describes a consistent pattern. Pursuits usually involve young men fleeing traffic stops or stops involving stolen vehicles. They tend to occur at night on local roads, last less than five minutes, and end when the driver stops, the officer terminates the pursuit, or a crash occurs [@alpert1988research; @alpert1989hot; @hoffmann2005pursuits; @crew1999assessing]. An estimated 20–40% end in a crash, 12–41% result in injury, and about 1% result in death [@alpert1988research; @kenney1997national]. Between 1994 and 2002, @rivara2004motor documented 2,654 fatal pursuit-related crashes in the United States (an average of 295 per year) resulting in 3,146 deaths. Of these, 1,048 (33.3%) were occupants of vehicles entirely uninvolved in the pursuit or pedestrians and cyclists. More recent national data show no improvement. Using Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) records from 2009 through 2023, @Hendrix2026 identified 5,425 fatal pursuit crashes and 6,352 deaths, or about 423 deaths per year. After accounting for population growth and overall crash frequency, they found that fatality risk rose by roughly 2% each year. The South had the highest rate and the Northeast the lowest. Fifty-seven percent of fatal crashes occurred in urban areas, and 70% occurred at night.

The Police Executive Research Forum (PERF), the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), and the Justice Department's Office of Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS Office) recently distilled this research into 65 recommendations [@perf2023vehicular]. The report's central principle is that pursuit policy should balance the risk of immediate apprehension failure against the danger to officers, suspects, and uninvolved bystanders. PERF's recommended default standard, which limits pursuits to violent crimes and situations posing an imminent threat to public safety, follows the restrictive model that emerged from the liability-driven reforms of the 1990s while placing it within an explicit risk-management framework.

The offense triggering a pursuit often does not justify the risks incurred. @hoffmann2005pursuits, for example, found that "very few apprehended drivers were charged with crimes more serious than what was known at the time the pursuit was initiated." However, @alpert1988research remind us that while it is true many pursuits begin with traffic violations, a nontrivial share of apprehended suspects are subsequently charged with serious felonies unrelated to the pursuit itself. This suggests that pursuits sometimes uncover criminality that would not otherwise have been detected, albeit at substantial cost.

## Theory and Evidence: Two Channels

Pursuit policy operates through two channels that differ in the strength of the causal claim each supports. Collisions follow mechanically from pursuit volume. Crime effects, by contrast, materialize only if pursuit escalation actually changes offender behavior — a harder identification problem, since within-city crime trends may reflect secular forces unrelated to pursuit policy. The theoretical mechanisms, the evidence base, and the identification burden differ accordingly, and this distinction organizes the discussion below.

### The Collision Channel

The argument to constrain officer discretion to pursue emphasizes the potential for collateral harms. Pursuits impose externalities on third parties who were not involved in the precipitating offense. @rivara2004motor found that 33.3% of pursuit fatalities were occupants of vehicles entirely uninvolved in the pursuit, pedestrians, or cyclists.^[The public has expressed ambivalence about this trade-off: @macdonald1998public found that while citizens support police pursuits in principle, support dwindles when pursuits involve minor offenses or result in bystander injuries. In a recent survey experiment, @mourtgos2026risk demonstrated that public judgments of pursuit appropriateness are sensitive to both the severity of the triggering offense and the risk to bystanders.] @rangehutson2007review documented similar patterns in a review of pursuit fatalities from 1982 through 2004.

Rigorous evaluation of how pursuit policy shapes this collision channel comes chiefly from a pair of natural experiments in the 1990s. When Dade County, Florida, restricted pursuits to violent felons in 1992, pursuit frequency dropped by 82% and pursuit-related injuries decreased, with no observed increase in crime rates or the number of suspects fleeing from police [@hoffmann2005pursuits; @alpert1994police]. Conversely, when Omaha, Nebraska, relaxed its pursuit policy in 1993, pursuit frequency increased by over 600% [@alpert1997constitutional]. These cases are suggestive, but they predate modern causal inference methods and lack rigorous comparison groups.

Recent evaluations have added more systematic evidence, including several pre-/post-test designs. The @policingproject2021roanoke conducted a formal cost-benefit analysis of policy changes in two Virginia jurisdictions, finding that Roanoke County's 2013 adoption of a restrictive policy reduced pursuit frequency and harm without measurable crime increases, while arrest rates for serious offenses were unchanged. @hosking2021policy examined two waves of reform in Queensland, Australia, documenting that restrictive policies reduced pursuit-related injuries without generating the crime consequences that critics predicted, though initial officer resistance weakened implementation. @butler2018milwaukee found that Milwaukee's 2017 policy liberalization led to a 155% increase in pursuits the following year, accompanied by a rise in pursuit-related collisions. @rivara2025washington studied pursuit outcomes in 64 Washington State agencies from 2019 through 2024. Pursuits often began with traffic violations and posed substantial injury risk. Because the state tightened its rules in 2021–2022 and partially reversed them in 2024, the study period spans several enforcement environments. @aronie2020blackjack synthesized the cumulative evidence to argue that the data "strongly favor a restrictive pursuit policy," noting that approximately 91% of pursuits are initiated for non-violent offenses and roughly 30% result in a crash. The evidence thus establishes the direction of the relationship. Policy affects pursuit volume, and pursuit volume affects harm. The question for the present study is how precisely those effects can be estimated.

### The Crime Channel

The case for broader pursuit authority rests primarily on deterrence theory. General deterrence holds that the credible threat of apprehension discourages potential offenders from fleeing and, more broadly, from committing crimes likely to bring them into contact with police [@senese1996pursue]. Specific deterrence holds that apprehended and sanctioned offenders are less likely to reoffend, having experienced the costs of criminal activity firsthand. Incapacitation provides a related but distinct mechanism. Arrest and detention temporarily remove suspects from the offending population, reducing crime during the period of confinement. Because pursuit escalation raises the perceived certainty of apprehension without altering sanction severity, it acts on precisely the margin the deterrence literature identifies as most likely to produce a behavioral response [@chalfin2017criminal; @nagin2013deterrence]. A null on this margin is therefore more informative than a null on severity would be.

Three complications qualify these mechanisms. First, deterrence through pursuit requires that potential offenders are aware of the prevailing policy and update their behavior accordingly. While formal policy changes may receive limited public attention, a visible, sustained increase in vehicle pursuits may communicate enforcement intensity through experiential channels even without formal announcements [@homant1994risk]. Second, the deterrence benefit of pursuits depends critically on the apprehension rate. If pursued suspects frequently escape, as they do in roughly 30% of cases [@alpert1988research], the deterrence signal is weakened. Third, deterrence theory assumes rational calculation by offenders, yet the population of fleeing drivers is disproportionately young, male, intoxicated, and unlicensed [@rivara2004motor], characteristics associated with impaired risk assessment.^[Research on perceptual deterrence provides more specific theoretical mechanisms for this limitation. @pogarsky2017heuristics demonstrated that potential offenders rely on cognitive heuristics (e.g., anchoring, availability, and question substitution) rather than coherent probability estimates, especially under time pressure. @barnum2021sanction further showed that person-specific cognitive biases can decouple perceived apprehension risk from actual enforcement intensity, a decoupling most acute for the young, impulsive, intoxicated population disproportionately represented among fleeing drivers.]

Only a handful of studies have examined how pursuit policies affect crime. @hicks2006police surveyed state-level pursuit policies and documented substantial variation in restrictiveness but did not link policy variation to outcomes. @wade2014highrisk developed a pursuit risk classification system but focused on individual pursuit characteristics rather than policy-level effects. @crew1999assessing attempted a cost-benefit framework for pursuit decisions but lacked the outcome data to conduct a full welfare analysis. Cataloging the 44 empirical pursuit studies conducted since 1970, @alpert2014pursuit reached a sobering conclusion: none had examined the effect of restrictive policies on general crime rates. Decades of research have documented pursuit patterns and outcomes without producing causal evidence on the question policymakers actually face.

Across these studies, restrictive policies consistently reduce pursuits and pursuit-related harm. The lack of accompanying crime spikes is suggestive, but it is not causal evidence. Prior work cannot distinguish a policy effect from a coincident secular crime decline. The NYPD's escalation, stabilization, and re-restriction within three years provide an unusually rich setting in which to address this gap.

## The NYPD Policy Change

The NYPD's pursuit escalation unfolded in three distinct phases. The first began in late 2022, alongside John Chell's appointment as Chief of Patrol in December and Mayor Adams's broader emphasis on quality-of-life enforcement. Monthly pursuits increased from 32 in November 2022 to 53 in December and 133 in January 2023, exceeding the combined total for 2018 and 2019. Crucially, no formal change to the department's written vehicle pursuit procedure (PG 212-39) accompanied this shift. Rather, the increase reflected an enforcement posture emphasizing aggressive pursuit of "ghost cars," ATVs, and vehicles with illegal plates. By the end of the first quarter of 2023, the NYPD recorded 304 pursuits, a roughly 600% increase over the same period the prior year. Chief Chell publicly defended the surge: “People thinking they can take off on us? Those days are over” [@brosnan2023nypd].

The second phase began in August 2023, when Chief of Department Jeffrey Maddrey circulated an internal memo reminding officers to follow existing Patrol Guide guidelines and emphasizing that pursuits "must be terminated when risks outweigh the danger of delayed apprehension" [@gonen2023nypd]. The memo listed relevant risk factors (e.g., nature of offense, time of day, weather, population density) and stressed supervisory responsibility and possible discipline for noncompliance. However, it did not narrow the offense categories that could trigger a pursuit. The memo therefore reinforced compliance rather than changing policy. Pursuit volume remained high throughout 2024, with quarterly counts approaching 600.

The third phase began in February 2025, when Commissioner Jessica Tisch implemented the first rewrite of the pursuit procedure since the pursuit surge began. The new policy restricted pursuits to felonies and violent misdemeanors, explicitly excluding traffic infractions, violations, and non-violent misdemeanors. It also protected officers from discipline for good-faith decisions to terminate a pursuit and imposed stricter risk-assessment requirements near homes, schools, and playgrounds. The NYPD reported that 67% of 2024 pursuits began when drivers fled traffic stops, scenarios that would no longer satisfy the revised criteria. Pursuits fell 66% in the first two weeks after implementation.

# Data and Methods

## Data Sources

We draw on five administrative data series from NYC Open Data. *Calls for service* records (January 2018 through December 2025) identify pursuit-related radio broadcasts, from which we aggregate monthly pursuit event counts. The ITS analysis window begins January 2018. *Motor vehicle collision* records (2016 through December 2025) report vehicle-level crash involvement; we collapse to the incident level and identify pursuit-related crashes using the pre-crash condition field, which designates "Police Pursuit" as the precipitating circumstance (an administrative classification applied by officers in the collision reporting system). *NYPD complaint data* (January 2014 through December 2025) provide monthly robbery complaint counts. *NYPD shooting incident data* (through December 2025) record victim-level shooting events; we deduplicate to the incident level using unique incident keys. *Shots-fired complaints* (beginning January 2018) capture incidents of gunfire in which no victim was struck. Table 1 summarizes annual totals for each outcome.

### Measures

All variables are measured at the monthly level. *Vehicle pursuit events* reflect counts of pursuit-related calls for service broadcasts, capturing the treatment itself (pre-escalation mean: `r round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_pursuits), 1)` events/month; post-Maddrey mean: `r round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Post-Maddrey", regime)) |> pull(mean_pursuits), 1)` events/month). *Pursuit-related motor vehicle collisions* capture incidents involving vehicles in pursuit situations (pre-escalation mean: `r round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_crashes), 1)` collisions/month). *Robberies* are drawn from complaint-level robbery reports (pre-escalation mean: `r comma(round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_robberies), 0))` complaints/month). *Shooting incidents* are from victim-level records (pre-escalation mean: `r round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_shootings), 1)` incidents/month). Finally, *total gun violence events* reflect the sum of shooting incidents and shots-fired reports (pre-escalation mean: `r round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_gun_events), 0)` events/month). We focus on robberies and shootings as our primary crime outcomes following both empirical convention and practitioner emphasis. NYPD Chief of Patrol John Chell explicitly linked expanded pursuit enforcement to these outcomes, stating that illegal vehicles "cause street violence — robberies and shootings" [@brosnan2023nypd].

## Analytic Strategy

We use segmented ITS to estimate collision effects. For crime, we combine city- and borough-level ITS, a 77-precinct panel, generalized synthetic control, and the February 2025 reversal. We treat the citywide ITS estimate as an upper bound rather than a causal estimate.

### Interrupted Time Series (ITS)

The segmented regression model is estimated on monthly data from January 2018 through December 2025 [@bernal2017interrupted; @wagner2002segmented]:

$$Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T + \beta_2 D_t + \beta_3 P_t + \sum_{m=2}^{12} \gamma_m \text{Month}_m + \delta \text{COVID}_t + \varepsilon_t$$

where $T$ is a linear time trend (months from start), $D_t$ is a binary indicator equal to 1 for months on or after October 2022, $P_t$ counts months elapsed since the intervention and equals 0 during the pre-intervention period, $\text{Month}_m$ terms are seasonal fixed effects, and $\text{COVID}_t$ flags the pandemic period (March 2020 through June 2021). The coefficient $\beta_2$ captures the immediate level shift at the intervention, while $\beta_3$ captures any change in the post-intervention slope. We estimate Newey-West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors with a lag of 6 months [@newey1987simple], computed via R's `sandwich` package. October 2022 is chosen as the intervention date because pursuit volume began its sustained rise in that month following Mayor Adams's quality-of-life enforcement mandate and Chief of Patrol Chell's operational directives; pursuit counts quadrupled from Q3 to Q4 2022 and continued rising through 2023. Sensitivity analyses presented in Appendix B confirm that key estimates are robust to moving the break date across September 2022 through January 2023 (one month before to three months after October 2022).

### Borough-Level Interrupted Time Series

To examine within-NYC heterogeneity in crime responses, we estimate the same segmented regression model separately for each of the five NYC boroughs:

$$Y_{bt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T + \beta_2 D_t + \beta_3 P_t + \sum_{m=2}^{12} \gamma_m \text{Month}_m + \delta \text{COVID}_t + \varepsilon_{bt}$$

where subscripts $b$ and $t$ denote borough and month, respectively. The specification is identical to the city-level ITS model, and Newey-West HAC standard errors are computed with lag = 6 throughout for comparability. Under deterrence, boroughs with larger increases in pursuits should show larger crime declines. We present this comparison and the precinct comparison below as descriptive: as the Results show, the groups being compared are not on parallel pre-treatment trajectories, so neither supports a causal estimate of the pursuit effect.

### Precinct-Level Panel Analysis

The policy change created citywide variation in pursuit exposure at the precinct level: when the department shifted enforcement posture in October 2022, which precincts actually used the new pursuit authority, and how intensively, depended on local crime patterns and operational circumstances. We describe this cross-sectional variation with a heterogeneous-effects difference-in-differences (DiD) design using a balanced panel of 77 NYPD precincts over 96 months (January 2018–December 2025; N = 7,392 precinct-months).^[Note that the 105th Precinct was split into two (the 105th and the 116th) in December 2024; for this analysis, we treat it as a single unit throughout the study period.]

**Heterogeneous-effects DiD design.** We classify precincts into high- and low-crime groups based on their mean monthly crime rate during the pre-October 2022 period, split at the median. The rationale is that precincts with higher pre-treatment crime rates are expected to have had greater tactical incentive to pursue fleeing suspects following the escalation (officers in high-crime areas face more pursuit-eligible situations), so baseline crime rate serves as a proxy for differential pursuit exposure. In the post-escalation period (October 2022–December 2025), high-robbery precincts averaged `r if (!is.null(pursuit_by_group_summary)) round(pursuit_by_group_summary |> filter(grouping_var=="robbery", group=="High robbery") |> pull(mean_pursuits), 1) else "[pending]"` pursuit broadcast events per month (SD = `r if (!is.null(pursuit_by_group_summary)) round(pursuit_by_group_summary |> filter(grouping_var=="robbery", group=="High robbery") |> pull(sd_pursuits), 1) else "[pending]"`), compared to `r if (!is.null(pursuit_by_group_summary)) round(pursuit_by_group_summary |> filter(grouping_var=="robbery", group=="Low robbery") |> pull(mean_pursuits), 1) else "[pending]"` (SD = `r if (!is.null(pursuit_by_group_summary)) round(pursuit_by_group_summary |> filter(grouping_var=="robbery", group=="Low robbery") |> pull(sd_pursuits), 1) else "[pending]"`) for low-robbery precincts, approximately twice the pursuit rate, consistent with the proxy assumption.^[This classification is constructed entirely from pre-intervention data and is therefore predetermined with respect to the policy change. Critically, using post-treatment pursuit counts as the grouping variable would be endogenous: pursuit intensity itself is an outcome of the policy, and precincts with higher crime would be expected to generate more pursuits under any enforcement posture. By fixing the grouping on pre-intervention crime rates, we ensure that the identifying contrast cannot be contaminated by post-treatment changes in pursuit behavior or crime dynamics.] Each outcome uses its own pre-treatment baseline (e.g., the robbery analysis groups precincts by their pre-treatment robbery rate). A supplementary quartile dose-response specification assigns precincts to quartiles Q1–Q4 and tests whether the post-treatment crime change varies linearly across the quartile ranking. The intervention date is October 2022 for all precincts, a common break reflecting the citywide policy change.

The DiD scalar estimate is:

$$Y_{pt} = \alpha_p + \lambda_t + \beta \cdot (\text{Post}_t \times \text{HighCrime}_p) + \varepsilon_{pt}$$

where $\alpha_p$ are precinct fixed effects, $\lambda_t$ are month-year fixed effects, and $\beta$ is the DiD estimate: the excess post-intervention change in crime for high-crime precincts relative to low-crime precincts. Standard errors are clustered at the precinct level (G = 77).

The DiD event study specification replaces the scalar interaction with a set of relative-time interactions:

$$Y_{pt} = \alpha_p + \lambda_t + \sum_{k \neq -1} \delta_k \cdot \mathbf{1}[q(t) - q(t_0) = k] \times \text{HighCrime}_p + \varepsilon_{pt}$$

where $q(t) = \lfloor t / 3 \rfloor$ maps the monthly time index $t$ to its quarterly bin, $t_0 =$ October 2022, and $k$ indexes quarterly bins relative to the intervention (each bin aggregates three consecutive calendar months), referenced at $k = -1$ (July–September 2022). The Tisch reversal period (January 2025 onward, with the policy taking effect in February 2025) is pooled into a single lump bin ($k = 9$).^[Bin $k = 9$ is anchored to the quarterly structure defined relative to the October 2022 intervention and so does not align exactly with the February 2025 effective date used for the post-Tisch regime elsewhere in this paper (see Event Study / Multi-Period Analysis below); it therefore includes January 2025 (one month of Post-Maddrey data) alongside the actual post-Tisch months. It also pools all months from January 2025 through the end of the study period, rather than a single quarter, to maintain adequate within-bin precinct-months near the end of the panel.] Pre-period $\delta_k$ coefficients near zero would confirm that high- and low-crime precincts were on parallel crime trajectories before the policy change, the key identifying assumption for this design. Post-period $\delta_k$ coefficients trace the divergence between groups over time. Standard errors are clustered at the precinct level (G = 77) throughout.

### Event Study / Multi-Period Analysis

We define four policy regimes to examine how outcomes evolved across distinct phases. The first is the *pre-escalation* period, which spans January 2018 to September 2022 and serves as our baseline. The second is the *escalation* period from October 2022 through July 2023, when pursuits surged. Third is the *post-Maddrey* phase, which begins with Chief of Department Jeffrey Maddrey's compliance memo in August 2023 and runs through January 2025. Finally, the *post-Tisch* phase begins with Commissioner Tisch's formal policy rewrite in February 2025 and runs through the end of our study period (December 2025).

### Generalized Synthetic Control

We apply the generalized synthetic control method (gsynth; @xu2017gsc) to panels of large U.S. cities to provide a national comparison for the shooting and robbery outcomes. The shooting panel uses monthly Gun Violence Archive counts as compiled by @sharkey2026american (January 2014 through December 2025); the robbery panel uses annual FBI Uniform Crime Reports counts [@kaplan2025ucr] for the 34 cities with complete 2014–2024 coverage. Gsynth generalizes difference-in-differences by fitting an interactive fixed effects model in which a data-selected number of latent factors load differently across units; when cross-validation selects zero factors, as it does here, the estimator reduces to two-way (unit and time) fixed effects. NYC is the single treated unit; the shooting donor pool excludes 24 cities with documented pursuit policy changes between 2018 and 2024 to avoid violations of the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA; see Appendix C for the full exclusion list). The number of latent factors is selected by leave-one-out cross-validation, and inference uses 500 parametric bootstrap iterations. As a robustness check, we replicate the shooting analysis with the full top-50-by-population donor panel (including cities with documented pursuit policy changes), which provides a conservative upper bound on the treatment estimate given the potential SUTVA contamination.

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

# Results

## Pursuit Activity

Monthly pursuit events increased sharply following the department's enforcement posture shift in late 2022. In the pre-escalation period (January 2018–September 2022), the NYPD averaged `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_pursuits)` pursuit events per month. Pursuit volume rose to a mean of `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_pursuits)` during the initial escalation phase (October 2022–July 2023) and continued climbing to `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Post-Maddrey", regime)) |> pull(mean_pursuits)` per month during the Post-Maddrey period (August 2023–January 2025), as the August 2023 compliance memo reinforced existing procedures without restricting eligible offenses. Annually, pursuit events totaled `r comma(table1 |> filter(year == 2023) |> pull(pursuits))` in 2023 and `r comma(table1 |> filter(year == 2024) |> pull(pursuits))` in 2024, compared with `r comma(table1 |> filter(year == 2022) |> pull(pursuits))` in 2022 (Table 1). The ITS model estimates an immediate level shift of *b*₂ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Pursuits") |> pull(estimate), 1)` events per month (SE = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Pursuits") |> pull(std.error), 1)`, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Pursuits") |> pull(p.value))`).

The February 2025 restriction reversed the escalation. Monthly pursuits fell from a pre-Tisch mean of `r table9 |> filter(outcome=="Pursuits") |> pull(pre_tisch_fmt)` to `r table9 |> filter(outcome=="Pursuits") |> pull(post_tisch_fmt)` (`r table9 |> filter(outcome=="Pursuits") |> pull(pct_change_fmt)`), consistent with the department's disclosure that approximately two-thirds of 2024 pursuits (most initiated when drivers fled traffic stops) would not qualify under the new felony-and-violent-misdemeanor threshold. Figure 1 illustrates pursuit volume across all four policy regimes.

```{r fig-regimes}
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(here("output", "plots", "event_regime_pursuit_events.png"))
```

Table 1 provides annual totals for each outcome across the full study period, offering a pre/post summary of how the key indicators changed alongside the pursuit escalation.

```{r table1}
#| label: tbl-annual
#| tbl-cap: "Annual Summary of Key Outcomes, 2018–2025"

table1 |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    pursuit_pct = case_when(
      is.na(pursuit_pct) ~ "—",
      pursuit_pct > 0 ~ paste0("+", round(pursuit_pct, 1), "%"),
      TRUE ~ paste0(round(pursuit_pct, 1), "%")
    ),
    collision_pct = case_when(
      is.na(collision_pct) ~ "—",
      collision_pct > 0 ~ paste0("+", round(collision_pct, 1), "%"),
      TRUE ~ paste0(round(collision_pct, 1), "%")
    ),
    robbery_pct = case_when(
      is.na(robbery_pct) ~ "—",
      robbery_pct > 0 ~ paste0("+", round(robbery_pct, 1), "%"),
      TRUE ~ paste0(round(robbery_pct, 1), "%")
    ),
    shooting_pct = case_when(
      is.na(shooting_pct) ~ "—",
      shooting_pct > 0 ~ paste0("+", round(shooting_pct, 1), "%"),
      TRUE ~ paste0(round(shooting_pct, 1), "%")
    ),
    gun_violence_pct = case_when(
      is.na(gun_violence_pct) ~ "—",
      gun_violence_pct > 0 ~ paste0("+", round(gun_violence_pct, 1), "%"),
      TRUE ~ paste0(round(gun_violence_pct, 1), "%")
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Year           = year,
    Pursuits       = pursuits,      `Δ Pursuits`      = pursuit_pct,
    Crashes        = collisions,    `Δ Crashes`       = collision_pct,
    Robberies      = robberies,     `Δ Robberies`     = robbery_pct,
    Shootings      = shootings,     `Δ Shootings`     = shooting_pct,
    `Gun Violence` = gun_violence,  `Δ Gun Violence`  = gun_violence_pct
  ) |>
  flextable() |>
  set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1) |>
  autofit()
```

## Pursuit-Related Collisions

Pursuit-related collisions increased substantially following the escalation (see Table 2). The ITS model estimates an immediate level shift of *b*₂ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Collisions") |> pull(estimate), 1)` additional collisions per month (SE = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Collisions") |> pull(std.error), 2)`, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Collisions") |> pull(p.value))`), with no significant change in the post-intervention slope (*p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="t_since", outcome=="Collisions") |> pull(p.value))`). Prior to the escalation, the NYPD averaged `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_crashes)` pursuit-related collisions per month; this rose to `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Post-Maddrey", regime)) |> pull(mean_crashes)` per month during the post-Maddrey period, a more than fivefold increase in total crash burden. Although the per-pursuit crash rate fell from `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(crash_rate)` to approximately `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Post-Maddrey", regime)) |> pull(crash_rate)` as lower-risk pursuits were added, the absolute collision toll increased substantially given the scale of the volume increase. The pre-escalation per-pursuit crash rate may also partly reflect administrative underreporting in earlier periods when pursuit tracking was less systematic, which would make the observed decline appear steeper than the underlying behavioral shift.

The per-pursuit rate decline reflects a compositional shift, not reduced harm. Pre-escalation pursuits were heavily selected (only situations serious enough to overcome institutional norms) and consequently ended in collisions at an elevated rate. As volume expanded after October 2022, the marginal pursuit increasingly involved lower-risk situations: fled traffic stops, ATV operators, vehicles with illegal plates. These added pursuits carry lower per-event crash probability, pulling the average rate down. The policy question turns on aggregate harm: a rate of `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Post-Maddrey", regime)) |> pull(crash_rate)` applied to approximately `r comma(round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Post-Maddrey", regime)) |> mutate(total = mean_pursuits * months) |> pull(total)))` Post-Maddrey pursuits generates far more collisions than `r table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(crash_rate)` applied to approximately `r round(table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> mutate(total = mean_pursuits * months) |> pull(total))` pre-escalation pursuits.

The multi-period event study corroborates this pattern closely. Collision counts trended upward throughout the escalation phase (*b* = `r round(table8 |> filter(outcome=="Collisions", term=="t_since_escalation") |> pull(estimate), 2)` per month, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(table8 |> filter(outcome=="Collisions", term=="t_since_escalation") |> pull(p.value))`), jumped at the start of the Post-Maddrey period (*b* = `r round(table8 |> filter(outcome=="Collisions", term=="post_maddrey") |> pull(estimate), 1)`, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(table8 |> filter(outcome=="Collisions", term=="post_maddrey") |> pull(p.value))`), and declined sharply following the February 2025 restriction (*b* = `r round(table8 |> filter(outcome=="Collisions", term=="post_tisch") |> pull(estimate), 1)`, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(table8 |> filter(outcome=="Collisions", term=="post_tisch") |> pull(p.value))`). This close correspondence across all four policy regimes is consistent with a direct causal mechanism.

## Crime Outcomes

We next examine whether the escalation reduced crime. The city-level interrupted time series and the national synthetic-control comparison, presented here, provide no evidence that the escalation reduced crime relative to the counterfactual; the re-restriction test and the community-level comparisons that follow point the same way.

### City-Level Interrupted Time Series

During the pre-intervention window, shooting incidents were trending upward at *b*₁ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="t", outcome=="Shootings") |> pull(estimate), 2)` incidents per month (*p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="t", outcome=="Shootings") |> pull(p.value))`); the counterfactual projection continues this upward trajectory, so the post-intervention estimates reflect deviations from an already-rising baseline. Shooting incidents declined relative to this counterfactual: the ITS estimates an immediate level shift of *b*₂ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Shootings") |> pull(estimate), 1)` incidents per month (SE = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Shootings") |> pull(std.error), 2)`, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Shootings") |> pull(p.value))`), with the post-intervention trend shifting further downward relative to the pre-intervention trend (*b*₃ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="t_since", outcome=="Shootings") |> pull(estimate), 2)` per month, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="t_since", outcome=="Shootings") |> pull(p.value))`). Aggregate gun violence (shootings plus shots-fired reports) declined similarly, with an immediate level shift of *b*₂ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Gun Violence") |> pull(estimate), 1)` (*p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Gun Violence") |> pull(p.value))`) and a comparable downward shift in the post-intervention trend (*b*₃ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="t_since", outcome=="Gun Violence") |> pull(estimate), 1)` per month, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="t_since", outcome=="Gun Violence") |> pull(p.value))`).

```{r table2a}
#| label: tbl-its
#| tbl-cap: "Interrupted Time Series Estimates (Newey-West HAC Standard Errors, Lag = 6)"

pre_means_tbl <- tibble(
  Outcome  = c("Pursuits", "Collisions", "Robberies", "Shootings", "Gun Violence"),
  pre_mean = c(
    table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_pursuits),
    table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_crashes),
    table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_robberies),
    table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_shootings),
    table7 |> filter(grepl("Pre-escalation", regime)) |> pull(mean_gun_events)
  )
)

its_pct <- its_nw |>
  filter(term %in% c("post", "t_since")) |>
  mutate(Term = if_else(term == "post", "Level shift", "Slope change"),
         Outcome = outcome) |>
  left_join(pre_means_tbl, by = "Outcome") |>
  mutate(`% of Baseline` = paste0(
    if_else(estimate / pre_mean * 100 >= 0, "+", ""),
    round(estimate / pre_mean * 100, 1), "%"
  )) |>
  select(Outcome, Term, `% of Baseline`)

table2a |>
  rename(
    Outcome       = outcome,
    Term          = term,
    Estimate      = estimate_fmt,
    `95% CI`      = ci,
    `p-value`     = p.value
  ) |>
  mutate(`p-value` = gsub("0\\.", ".", format.pval(`p-value`, digits = 3, eps = .001))) |>
  left_join(its_pct, by = c("Outcome", "Term")) |>
  select(Outcome, Term, Estimate, `% of Baseline`, `95% CI`, `p-value`) |>
  flextable() |>
  footnote(j = "% of Baseline", part = "header",
           value = as_paragraph(
             "Estimate as a percentage of the pre-escalation monthly mean for that outcome. "),
           ref_symbols = "a") |>
  set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1) |>
  autofit()
```

Robbery showed no immediate change (*b*₂ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Robberies") |> pull(estimate), 1)`, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="post", outcome=="Robberies") |> pull(p.value))`), but the post-intervention trend shifted sharply downward relative to the pre-intervention trend (*b*₃ = `r round(its_nw |> filter(term=="t_since", outcome=="Robberies") |> pull(estimate), 1)` per month, *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(its_nw |> filter(term=="t_since", outcome=="Robberies") |> pull(p.value))`), indicating a gradual trajectory shift. The 2022 pre-intervention robbery trend itself reflected the post-COVID normalization noted above and was not uniform across the city, which shapes the pre-period baseline against which the ITS projects forward. Intervention date sensitivity analyses confirm that the key estimates are robust to moving the treatment date from one month earlier to three months later (September 2022 through January 2023). Pre-period placebo tests (within-NYC temporal placebos) produce no comparable signals, ruling out spurious detection within the analysis window; these tests do not, however, rule out national crime-trend confounding. Three concurrent confounders are most plausible: the April 2023 New York State bail reform amendments that restored pretrial detention authority for certain offenses, post-COVID crime normalization following NYC's 2021 shooting peak, and successive NYPD leadership and strategy changes between 2022 and 2025. The ITS crime estimates should therefore be read as an upper bound on potential deterrence benefits rather than as causal estimates; the generalized synthetic control (next subsection) provides the most direct test of whether the ITS crime decline outpaced national trends, and it did not. Figure 2 displays the segmented regression fits for all four outcomes.

```{r fig-its}

#| fig-cap: "Interrupted time series segmented regression fits for four outcomes, January 2018–December 2025. Top row: pursuit-related collisions (left) and shooting incidents (right). Bottom row: aggregate gun violence, shootings plus shots-fired reports (left), and robberies (right). Solid line: segmented regression fit. Dashed line: counterfactual projected from the pre-intervention trend. Shaded band: the estimated post-intervention effect. Dotted vertical line: the October 2022 intervention. Points: observed monthly counts. Newey-West HAC standard errors (lag = 6)."
#| out-width: "100%"
```

### National Comparison: Generalized Synthetic Control

The within-NYC designs are each limited by the absence of a credible control city. The generalized synthetic control addresses this by constructing a weighted composite of large U.S. cities as NYC's counterfactual crime trajectory. Our primary outcome is the annualized shooting rate per 100,000 population from Gun Violence Archive data, observed monthly from January 2014 through December 2025; we also estimate the model for robbery. Gun violence as defined elsewhere in this paper, shootings plus shots-fired reports, has no counterpart in the national donor data, which record shootings only, so nationally the gun-violence question reduces to the shooting result. NYC is the single treated unit; all other cities serve as the donor pool.

**Design.** Leave-one-out cross-validation over $r = 0$–5 latent factors selects the specification; inference uses 500 parametric bootstrap iterations. The covariance matrix was singular in the F-test, which is expected with a single treated unit and does not affect point estimates or bootstrap confidence intervals [@xu2017gsc]. To avoid SUTVA contamination (donor cities whose shooting trends were themselves affected by their own pursuit policy changes), we exclude 24 cities with documented city-level or binding state-level pursuit policy changes between 2018 and 2024 (Appendix C). The resulting SUTVA-clean donor pool comprises `r gsynth_clean$n_donors` cities with stable pursuit policies, observed across `r gsynth_clean$n_months` months. As a robustness check, we replicate the analysis with the full top-50-by-population panel (`r gsynth_full$n_donors` donors). For robbery, the only national donor series available at the city level is annual (FBI Uniform Crime Reports, 2014–2024; `r gsynth_rob$n_donors` cities with complete data [@kaplan2025ucr]), so the robbery model is estimated on an annual panel with NYC's five boroughs aggregated to a single unit. Its `r gsynth_rob$n_post` post-treatment years make it a supporting comparison rather than a primary estimate.

**Results.** Cross-validation selects $r = `r gsynth_clean$n_factors`$ latent factors for the SUTVA-clean panel, so the estimator reduces to a two-way (city and month) fixed-effects comparison of NYC against the donor pool; the pre-treatment root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE) is `r round(gsynth_clean$pre_rmspe, 2)` per 100,000. The estimated average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) is `r round(gsynth_clean$att, 2)` shooting incidents per 100,000 (annualized), and none of the `r gsynth_clean$n_post` post-treatment months reaches significance at the .05 level. Figure 3 plots NYC's actual shooting rate against the gsynth counterfactual, and Figure 4 shows the period-by-period ATT gap; the 95% bootstrap confidence interval includes zero throughout the post-treatment window. A full-panel robustness check ($r = `r gsynth_full$n_factors`$, `r gsynth_full$n_donors` donors) yields a similarly null ATT of `r round(gsynth_full$att, 2)` per 100,000.^[Cross-validation under the current `gsynth` version selects $r = `r gsynth_clean$n_factors`$. Forcing $r = 3$, the specification an earlier `gsynth` version selected for these data, yields an ATT of `r round(gsynth_att |> filter(grepl("Previous-round", donor_pool)) |> pull(att), 2)` per 100,000 (95% CI [`r round(gsynth_att |> filter(grepl("Previous-round", donor_pool)) |> pull(ci_lower), 1)`, `r round(gsynth_att |> filter(grepl("Previous-round", donor_pool)) |> pull(ci_upper), 1)`]), likewise not distinguishable from zero.] Both specifications point to the same conclusion: NYC's post-October 2022 shooting trajectory is statistically indistinguishable from the national-trend counterfactual.

Following the recommendation of @abadie2015comparative for comparative synthetic-control studies, inference about the presence of an effect rests primarily on placebo-in-space permutation tests rather than the model-based bootstrap interval reported above. We re-estimate the SUTVA-clean gsynth model with each donor city treated in turn as the pseudo-treated unit, then rank NYC's own average post-treatment ATT and its pre/post mean-squared-prediction-error (MSPE) ratio against this donor-city distribution. NYC's ATT ranks `r gsynth_perm_att$rank` of `r gsynth_perm_att$n_valid` cities (two-sided permutation *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(gsynth_perm_att$p_value)`), and its MSPE ratio ranks `r gsynth_perm_mspe$rank` of `r gsynth_perm_mspe$n_valid` (one-sided permutation *p* `r fmt_p_stmt(gsynth_perm_mspe$p_value)`); both are squarely within the distribution expected if NYC's shooting trajectory were no different from an arbitrary donor city's. The permutation test corroborates the bootstrap-based null result without relying on the bootstrap's distributional assumptions.

**Robbery.** On the annual panel, cross-validation again selects zero factors. The estimated ATT is `r round(gsynth_rob$att, 1)` robberies per 100,000, or about `r round(gsynth_rob$att_pct)`% of NYC's pre-escalation robbery rate. The positive point estimate means that NYC's robbery rate rose relative to the synthetic control rather than falling (95% bootstrap CI [`r round(gsynth_rob$ci_lower, 1)`, `r round(gsynth_rob$ci_upper, 1)`]). The pre-treatment fit shows NYC's robbery rate already diverging upward from the donor pool before October 2022, the same non-parallel-trend pattern documented for the community-level comparisons below, so the robbery estimate carries the same caveat. It provides no evidence of a deterrent effect on robbery and, if anything, points the other way.

**What the comparison can rule out.** Because the headline national result is a null, the relevant question is how large a true effect it could have missed. Table 3 states each estimate and its 95% confidence interval as a percentage of NYC's own pre-escalation base rate. The shooting comparison is imprecise: the interval reaches roughly two times the baseline shooting rate in either direction, so on its own it cannot exclude a moderately sized deterrent effect. That imprecision follows from the outcome itself: shootings are comparatively rare, and the annualized city-level rate is volatile, so even the two-way fixed-effects counterfactual leaves a pre-treatment prediction error near `r round(national_mde |> filter(outcome=="Shootings", panel=="monthly") |> pull(rmspe_mde_pct))`% of the base rate. The robbery interval, for an outcome roughly 10 times more common, is correspondingly tighter: it runs from `r round(national_mde |> filter(outcome=="Robbery") |> pull(ci_lower_pct))`% to `r round(national_mde |> filter(outcome=="Robbery") |> pull(ci_upper_pct))`% of the base rate and rules out a robbery reduction larger than about two-fifths of the base rate. For each outcome the point estimate is at or above zero. The precision to exclude a small deterrent effect therefore comes not from any single national interval but from the convergence of evidence: the near-zero and wrong-signed point estimates here, the placebo-in-space test, the within-NYC time series, and the re-restriction that produced no crime rebound.

```{r tbl-mde}
#| label: tbl-mde
#| tbl-cap: "National Comparison Estimates as a Percentage of NYC's Pre-Escalation Base Rate"

national_mde |>
  filter((outcome == "Shootings" & panel == "monthly") | outcome == "Robbery") |>
  transmute(
    Outcome            = paste0(outcome, " (", panel, " panel)"),
    `Base rate (/100k)` = sprintf("%.1f", base_rate),
    `ATT (/100k)`       = sprintf("%+.1f", att),
    `ATT (% of base)`   = sprintf("%+.0f%%", att_pct),
    `95% CI (/100k)`    = sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", ci_lower, ci_upper),
    `95% CI (% of base)` = sprintf("[%+.0f%%, %+.0f%%]", ci_lower_pct, ci_upper_pct)
  ) |>
  flextable() |>
  set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1) |>
  autofit()
```

Dashed line: gsynth counterfactual constructed from ", gsynth_clean$n_donors, " SUTVA-clean donor cities. Vertical dotted line marks the October 2022 pursuit escalation.")'
